Q62572068.summary: This cast bronze belt plate is crowded with small figures in shallow relief. At the right a rider sits on a donkey whose head bends down toward a figure who stoops before it, as if spreading a garment on the road; standing figures look on at the left, and above, a row of heads looks out from an arcade. Read by the museum as Christ's Entry into Jerusalem, it shows how the Gospel story was carried into the everyday ornament of the early medieval peoples of the Alpine region.
facts: The buckle was found at La Roche-sur-Foron in Haute-Savoie and is in the Germanic antiquities collection of Geneva's Musée d'Art et d'Histoire (inv. E 0321).
Q62572068.notes: Identification, date (6th–7th century) and findspot are from the Wikidata item and the Commons file (photographed with the museum label); no MAH online record was consulted. The figure on the donkey is not haloed and the identification follows the museum's interpretation.
Q62572068.original_title: Boucle de ceinture en bronze Entrée dans Jérusalem

Q60751791.summary: Christ hangs on the cross at the centre of this walrus-ivory plaque, with busts of the sun and moon above the cross-arm. The soldier with the lance strides in from the left and the sponge-bearer with his bucket from the right, while two haloed mourners, the veiled Virgin at the left, stand at the edges. Though tiny, the scene gathers every element of the Passion around the crucified Christ.
facts: It belongs with three plaques of Christ in Majesty and the apostles from the same portable altar; the Cleveland Museum bought those from Emile Rey of Arnold Seligmann, Rey and Company, which donated this Crucifixion plaque later the same year (1922).
The plaque is only about 5.1 × 9.6 cm.

cur:catacombs2-arles-saint-trophime-two-.summary: Fourteen small arcades on two levels, divided by spiral-fluted columns, frame a sequence of biblical scenes on this mid-fourth-century sarcophagus. In the lower register, at the far left, Christ (now headless) stands before the swathed figure of Lazarus in his tomb, and further along a woman kneels at the feet of a figure in a toga, a familiar shorthand for Christ's healing miracles; a veiled orant, the praying soul of the deceased, stands at the centre. On the right short side, carved in continuous relief, the Magi bring their gifts to the Virgin and Child and Christ rides into Jerusalem on a donkey.
facts: According to the Commons description by Jean-Pol Grandmont, the sarcophagus came from the church of Saint-Honorat des Alyscamps, served as the high altar until the 18th century and then as a baptismal font in Saint-Trophime.

The French Wikipedia article on the sarcophagi of Arles singles it out as a composition that breaks with the continuous friezes of earlier work: two superposed registers subdivided by columns and arcades, datable to the mid-4th century.
It is a classified historic monument (Palissy PM13000293).
cur:catacombs2-arles-saint-trophime-two-.notes: Many heads are lost, so several scenes are identified only from their composition (Lazarus at lower left; the kneeling woman, probably the woman with an issue of blood). The Magi and the Entry into Jerusalem are on the right short side, visible in other photographs in the Commons category.

cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-blind-wido.summary: In the upper register, labelled in Greek, Christ anoints the eyes of the man born blind, who then bends to wash in the pool of Siloam while an angel hovers above; to the right Christ watches as the poor widow drops her two small coins into the tall temple treasury. Below, friends let a paralysed man down through a roof to Christ, who sits among the crowd. The page joins Christ's healing power to his praise of humble generosity.
facts: The Greek captions read 'Christ healing the man blind from birth', 'the pool of Siloam' and 'the widow with the two mites'.
The Paris Gregory was commissioned by Patriarch Photios as a gift for Emperor Basil I between 879 and 883.
cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-blind-wido.notes: Folio derived from the Gallica image sequence (view number minus 13, halved) and checked against folios named on other Commons files of this manuscript. The lower register is partly damaged.

cur:objects-berlin-crucifixion-with-dono.summary: Christ hangs on the cross beneath a starry sky with two mourning angels, the Virgin standing at the left and St John at the right. At the foot of the cross a small figure kneels in prostration, the donor who commissioned the relief, placing himself literally beneath the saving cross. The image joins the universal mystery of Calvary with one person's plea for mercy.
facts: Donor portraits in proskynesis (full prostration) at the foot of the cross or before Christ are a recurring feature of Middle Byzantine devotional objects (type).

cur:objects-bargello-casket-busts-christ.summary: This wooden casket is clad with ivory plaques showing busts of Christ, the Virgin and saints in arched frames, separated by bands of rosettes. Arranged like the figures of a templon screen, the holy persons turn the box into a small reliquary or treasure chest guarded by Christ and his saints. Byzantine workshops produced both secular rosette caskets and religious ones like this.
facts: 'Rosette caskets' with borders of carved rosettes were made in Constantinople mainly in the 10th and 11th centuries; most show mythological subjects, making religious examples rarer (type).

vam:O93842.summary: Carved in relief from dark green jasper, Christ stands full-length on a footstool within an arched field, bearded and with a cross-nimbus, raising his right hand in blessing and holding a jewelled Gospel book in his left. The stone is set in a gold mount with a suspension loop and a fleur-de-lis finial, so that it could be worn as a pendant. Small and precious, it is a personal devotional image from the court culture of Constantinople.
facts: An inscription on the reverse refers to the Emperor Leo VI (reigned 886–912), which gives the cameo its date (V&A).

The V&A notes that Byzantine cameos of Christ, the Virgin and popular saints were made in good numbers in semi-precious stones; being easily portable, several were later set into western book covers and reliquaries.
vam:O93842.notes: The worklist thumbnail (2006BG0359) is a group photograph of four V&A cameos; this object is the standing Christ in the arched gold mount at lower left. The same group image is used for vam:O96313 (lower right) and vam:O125665 (upper right). No single-object photograph of this cameo was found among the V&A images (the others are archive album pages). The mount is presumably later; the V&A does not date it.

wga:zearly/2/2paintin/5oberze3.summary: Christ, larger than those around him and followed by his disciples, steps in from the left and reaches out toward a man whose swollen belly marks him as suffering from dropsy; companions support the sick man before a gateway and the walls of a city. Pale blues, ochres and reds set the figures against fantastical buildings, and a perspective meander frames the scene. The Latin inscription beneath begins 'Obvius occurrens sanatur ydropicus', telling how the man who came to meet Christ was healed.
facts: The nave of St. Georg preserves one of the very few surviving painted cycles of Christ's miracles from before the year 1000 north of the Alps; this scene is the second on the north wall.
In almost every scene Christ enters from the left, so the cycle reads in sequence from the entrance toward the altar and back.
The date is disputed: most scholars favour the late 10th century, while some argue for c. 900 under Abbot Hatto III.
wga:zearly/2/2paintin/5oberze3.notes: WGA's generic title 'The Healing of the Sick' corrected from the inscription and from German Wikipedia's list of scenes ('Heilung des Wassersüchtigen'). Medium given as wall painting since the technique (true fresco or secco) was not verified.
